title: Deindividuation
description: In large groups or anonymous situations, people lose their sense of individual identity and responsibility. This can lead to behaviors they would never do alone—both positive (losing inhibitions at a concert) and negative (mob violence).
shortDescription: In large groups or anonymous situations, people lose their sense of individual identity and responsibility. This can lead to behaviors they would never do alone—both positive (losing inhibitions at a concert) and negative (mob violence).

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: In large groups or anonymous situations, people lose their sense of individual identity and responsibility. This can lead to behaviors they would never do alone—both positive (losing inhibitions at a concert) and negative (mob violence).

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A peaceful protest turns destructive when some people in the crowd start smashing windows; others follow because they feel invisible.
Online trolling: people say horrific things under anonymous accounts they’d never say face‑to‑face.
A normally shy employee shouts wildly at a sports game while wearing face paint.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Acting on impulse without considering consequences.
Following the group’s lead without personal reflection.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I don’t know what came over me.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: The environment is chaotic, and norms are unclear.
You’re in a large group where your individual actions can’t be traced.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Anonymity and group size weaken self‑awareness and fear of judgment. Zimbardo (1969) found that deindividuated participants administered longer shocks. The mask, the uniform, the crowd all reduce the sense of individual accountability.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: If you’re in a crowd that starts acting destructively, focus on your own name and identity. Remind yourself: “I am still me.”
Leaders can reduce deindividuation by calling people by name or making eye contact.
Online, always imagine the person reading your comment.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming deindividuation only causes bad behavior. It can also cause joyful abandon, but the destructive form is the one to watch.
Thinking “I’d never get swept up.” Most people are capable under the right circumstances.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A corporate office has a ritual “roast” of a departing colleague. What starts as friendly teasing turns brutal when the whole department piles on, each person trying to outdo the last. The colleague leaves humiliated. Later, participants individually feel ashamed and say, “I don’t know why I went along.”

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The crowd has no conscience; it borrows yours. When you can’t be singled out, you’re more likely to do what you’d never do alone.
